sources.headline: India’s Voter Roll Protests Swell
sources.text:
Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.
The highlights this week: Thousands of people protest India’s voter roll revision despite government crackdown, Pakistan’s government enacts emergency rule in opposition stronghold of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and a ruling party lawmaker in Nepal faces blackmail accusations.
Modi Faces Down New Protests
Thousands of protesters converged on New Delhi over the weekend to demand the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, India’s chief election commissioner. Opponents accuse Kumar of overseeing a manipulated voter roll revision that improves electoral prospects for the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The government insists that only those who don’t belong on the rolls were removed.
On Oct. 10, security forces in New Delhi detained as many as 7,000 people, and authorities closed metro stations and shut off mobile internet services. The protests, coming on the heels of mass protests against India’s education policies this summer, threaten to become the biggest sustained street mobilization against Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his 12 years in power.
The protests—taking place in large cities across the country—are unlikely to die down anytime soon, but it’s worth putting the movement in perspective.
Though tens of thousands of people have mobilized so far, in a country of India’s size, this doesn’t equate to a truly national mass movement. More Indians protested against sexual assault in 2012 and 2013 and corruption in 2011—all during the rule of Modi’s predecessor, former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh of the Indian National Congress party.
There is also a big difference between the demonstrations in India and the mass movements that ousted governments in Bangladesh, Nepal, and Sri Lanka in recent years: Modi’s government remains popular. Though many Indians—especially young ones—are increasingly angry about misgovernance and economic stress, a critical mass of the population still backs Modi.
However, Modi can’t simply shrug off the ongoing protests and assume that things will settle down. To start, the protesters have ample momentum, and many of them are part of the Cockroach Janta Party, which spearheaded the demonstrations that led to the resignation of India’s education minister in July. That marked a rare case of the Modi government giving in to protest demands.
That galvanized the protesters, who believe that they can be successful this time, too. The government’s heavy-handed tactics against the protests will likely prompt them to double down rather than dial back their efforts. Those targeted by the state, including Cockroach leaders detained over the weekend, have defiantly declared their commitment to staying in the streets.
From the protesters’ perspective, there is a tremendous amount at stake. They say the voter roll revision, which removed around 130 million names, will benefit the BJP by eliminating potential votes against the ruling party, particularly among members of India’s Muslim community. The changes come at a key electoral moment: Seven states go to the polls in 2027.
Among them are Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state and its biggest electoral prize, as well as Goa, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Manipur, Himachal Pradesh, and Modi’s home state of Gujarat. Based on total electorate data from the country’s 2024 general elections, this equates to around 30 percent of the country’s total voter base.
New Delhi faces a tough choice. Giving in to protesters would likely embolden them to demand more. But if Modi’s government rejects their concerns, demonstrators could grow angrier—and the movement could grow larger.
The voter roll protests don’t threaten the government’s hold on power. But assuming that they become sustained, Modi might need to take certain steps to reassert that hold on power, starting with reassuring coalition partners who feel uneasy about the pressure from the streets.
What We’re Following
Pakistan imposes emergency in opposition stronghold. Pakistan’s government enacted emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday, effectively placing it under Islamabad’s control. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi was detained, along with some of his cabinet ministers.
Islamabad justified the move based on what it described as the provincial government’s inability to curb terrorism. That is a likely pretext for a political move, however: Pakistan’s powerful military oversees counterterrorism policy in practice, and Afridi and his government belong to the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party led by imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan.
PTI launched a “long march” this month from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa toward Islamabad, intended to pressure the government to free Khan. Pakistan’s leadership likely imposed emergency rule to make it more difficult for PTI members and supporters to mobilize in the province and to put the party on the back foot as it looks to build momentum for its march.
Nepali MP denies blackmail allegations. A lawmaker with Nepal’s ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), Khagendra Sunar, has denied blackmail allegations after media outlet Jana Aastha reported allegations that Sunar is featured in an audio recording that suggests that he offered marriage to a woman, produced an explicit video, and then threatened to blackmail her.
Sunar insists that the recording is generated by artificial intelligence and that he is being targeted for raising concerns about corruption within the police. Nepali law enforcement officials are expected to investigate.
The case is notable given that the reformist RSP swept into power in March with a platform almost exclusively focused on anti-corruption. This isn’t the first time that a party member has faced similar allegations; RSP Chairman Rabi Lamichhane was charged with embezzlement in 2024. But Sunar’s case is one of the first since the RSP took over the government.
The only other publicized case involved Nepali Interior Minister Sudan Gurung stepping down during the initial days of the administration amid concerns about his financial activities. Gurung was later reinstated after an investigation found that he did nothing wrong.
Nuclear power in Bangladesh. The Rooppur nuclear power facility in Bangladesh achieved a milestone on Sunday, undertaking a controlled chain reaction for the first time—a key step to becoming fully operational that is known as “first criticality.” Once it is up and running, the Rooppur facility is projected to supply more than 10 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand.
This is significant for a couple reasons. The facility could eventually give Bangladesh, suffering a severe energy crisis, an energy security boost. Nuclear power could become a badly needed alternative fuel for a country that is heavily dependent on hydrocarbon imports from the Middle East and has made little headway in developing clean energy resources.
At the same time, the Rooppur facility is heavily funded by Russia, which is reportedly financing nearly $12 billion in loans—close to the total estimated value of the project. This means that progress on the facility could result in friction between Bangladesh and the United States at a moment when their bilateral relationship is strikingly smooth.
FP’s Most Read This Week
China Doesn’t Need to Invade Taiwan to Control It by Michael Poznansky and Ian Easton
Russian Sabotage in Europe Is No Longer ‘Symbolic’ by Sam Skove
To Understand France’s Unrest, Look Back to 1982 by Howard W. French
Under the Radar
The International Olympic Committee has announced the seven finalists to host the 2036 Summer Olympics—and India is one of them. The group will be winnowed down to a short list by March. The other finalists are Germany, Hungary, Qatar, South Africa, South Korea, and Turkey.
India has never hosted the Olympics, and it would appear to be a strong candidate, given its status as the world’s most populous country and one of its largest economies. It also has experience putting on major global sporting events: It hosted the Commonwealth Games in 2010 and is expected to do so again in 2030.
However, India’s candidacy will face challenges. Its management of the 2010 Commonwealth Games—four years before Modi took office—was heavily criticized for corruption and profligate spending. There will also be concerns about health and sanitation, especially water quality, as well as air pollution.
If India lands the 2036 Olympic Games, it would be a major coup and an opportunity to showcase to the world some of its major achievements—from digitization to infrastructure development.

sources.headline: Modi’s Crackdown Is a Strategic Error
sources.text:
Recent scenes in New Delhi evoke memories of past security crackdowns across South Asia, mostly by military dictators fighting to hang onto their regime. Beginning on Oct. 10, security forces swept thousands of people off the streets of India’s capital in a frantic attempt to suppress a surging citizens’ movement.
Estimates placed the number of those detained on that day alone at more than 7,000, among them opposition politicians, former chief ministers, student leaders, senior lawyers, and journalists. They had come out to protest the removal of more than 130 million names from voter rolls by the Indian Election Commission under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) that began last year.
Recent scenes in New Delhi evoke memories of past security crackdowns across South Asia, mostly by military dictators fighting to hang onto their regime. Beginning on Oct. 10, security forces swept thousands of people off the streets of India’s capital in a frantic attempt to suppress a surging citizens’ movement.
Estimates placed the number of those detained on that day alone at more than 7,000, among them opposition politicians, former chief ministers, student leaders, senior lawyers, and journalists. They had come out to protest the removal of more than 130 million names from voter rolls by the Indian Election Commission under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) that began last year.
Ahead of the Oct. 10 protest, authorities shut down 57 metro stations, canceled trains, and suspended mobile internet services in parts of New Delhi. More than 30,000 paramilitary troopers have now been deployed to the capital. Some of these forces were seen violently dragging demonstrators to police vans, including members of Parliament. Evidence of excessive force circulated widely online.
Despite the crackdown, thousands of people continued to turn up in New Delhi to protest with greater vigor. These demonstrations, galvanized in part by a youth-led movement, have escalated into a broader referendum on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Confronted with political fatigue, a falling rupee, and foreign-policy disappointments, Modi’s government has abandoned political engagement in favor of this theater of state coercion.
With formal democratic institutions weakened, tens of thousands of Indians are in the streets—seemingly recognizing that defending the vote is an existential fight for their democracy. Whether Modi navigates this volatile turning point through dialogue or further authoritarian overreach could determine not only his next few years but also India’s democratic trajectory.
The immediate demand of the ongoing protests, which have spread to other major Indian cities, is the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, whom Modi nominated to the panel in 2024, after a new law granting full executive control to appoint the election commissioners. In addition to the chief election commissioner, there are two deputies of equal standing who work with him.
Though opposition parties have complained about the deletion of voters since last year, a recent Indian Express investigation into the other commissioners’ objections to Kumar’s conduct, as well as the success of the fledgling Cockroach Janta Party movement, provided fresh impetus to the cause. In July, the Cockroach movement forced the resignation of India’s education minister over leaked examination papers. Those summer protests seemed to reveal the limits of Modi’s power, and calls for Kumar’s resignation have now become a lightning rod for wider frustration over economic discontent and democratic backsliding.
This confrontation arrives as Modi faces a political setting different from that of his first two terms, when he enjoyed absolute parliamentary dominance. The 2024 national elections were a setback, stripping Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) down to 240 seats in Parliament and making him govern in coalition. This year, Modi failed to push through important legislative measures, such as the expansion and redistricting of parliamentary seats. He retains the coercive power of the state but has lost the cushion that allowed him to ignore or isolate public dissent.
The Modi government’s reliance on police and paramilitary forces as the sole interface between the state and agitating citizens as it approaches the current protests is a crucial strategic error. Slogans and posters reveal that the youth see this as evidence of a frightened ruler hiding behind security forces. Though no pellet guns were fired this time, the heavily armed security personnel appeared to have been given a free hand to deal with the protesters.
This violent escalation has deepened public hostility and radicalized ordinary citizens; it risks escalating disparate street protests into wider civic defiance. More crucially, Modi’s continued silence over police violence is eroding his democratic and political legitimacy. By appearing to rule purely through force, he sacrifices the moral authority of a leader with popular consent; this alienates moderate voters and signals a government in retreat.
After the 2014 election, which the BJP won in a landslide, Modi’s authority was manufactured by an echo chamber of friendly media conglomerates. But shifting media consumption habits toward independent digital platforms and social media have rendered Modi’s legacy media control increasingly useless. The government’s communication machinery and its allied news networks no longer dictate the national narrative. It is no surprise then that the police picked up at least 37 journalists during the protests over the weekend.
After more than 12 years in power, Modi also faces political fatigue. Blaming past governments for current failures no longer resonates with an electorate in a country where more than half the population is under 25. These young Indians have no adult memory of another prime minister. Every voter removed from the list, every unkept promise on employment, and every instance of police overreach belong entirely to the incumbent leader.
Having personalized the government in unprecedent ways, Modi cannot deflect responsibility for the economic and political distress that Indians are now experiencing. This hopelessness about the future is recorded in recent government surveys. In one September poll, nearly half of respondents complained that employment conditions had worsened in the last year, while 35.5 percent expected the situation to further deteriorate in the next year.
This perspective is compounded by news of India’s macroeconomic stress. In 2026 so far, foreign portfolio investors have pulled a record $33 billion out of Indian equities, nearly double the entire 2025 outflow—a massive capital flight. Driven by global volatility and growth concerns, the rupee has depreciated more than 6.5 percent against the U.S. dollar this year, cementing it as one of Asia’s worst-performing currencies.
Despite the country’s official annualized GDP growth rate of 7.8 percent last quarter, these data points undercut the claim by official economic promotion agencies that India under Modi is a preferred destination for global capital.
Simultaneously, Modi’s foreign policy—long advertised as his signature strength—is fraying. Relations with the United States during President Donald Trump’s second term feature high tariffs (with threats of higher tariffs) and a stalled bilateral trade deal. A recent Pew Research Center survey shows that 50 percent of U.S. adults hold an unfavorable view of India, compared with the 45 percent who hold a favorable opinion. Having projected his comfort with Trump and having put New Delhi firmly on Washington’s side, Modi is now struggling to justify his choices.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration is increasingly treating Beijing as a peer. Modi finds himself squeezed from both sides, as China shows no inclination to resolve border tensions with India, share technology, or reduce their high trade deficit. The normalcy in ties with China that Modi desperately seeks after being rebuffed by Trump is only happening on Beijing’s terms. And as India’s West Asia policy of aligning with Israel and the United Arab Emirates backfires amid the Iran war, Modi finds himself further boxed in.
The deeper problem is institutional. Citing severe restrictions on civil society and the co-option of the judiciary, the Varieties of Democracy project places India’s electoral democracy score at 0.38, its lowest level since the official Emergency of 1975, and classifies it as an “electoral autocracy.” Freedom House rates India only partly free, giving the country its lowest-ever score this year. In its latest report, International IDEA also flags declines in judicial independence and the freedom of political parties in the country.
These assessments follow the same pattern in which the autonomy of the Election Commission has also been systematically eroded. When formal institutions of accountability cease to function, the street becomes the arena where ordinary people can assert agency and demand accountability. Moreover, in a country marked by deep socioeconomic inequality, the vote is only venue where every adult citizen is equal.
Loss of confidence in the integrity of that mechanism threatens not only access to state benefits for the poor but also the sense of democratic dignity that the franchise has provided since India’s independence in 1947. Stripped of institutional recourse, people recognize that losing the vote means losing their citizenship in practice. This explains why thousands of Indians are facing down police batons and detention rather than quietly retreating.
The future of Indian democracy hangs in a delicate balance as institutional guardrails face unprecedented stress tests. Whether Modi follows the trajectory of leaders such as Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan or former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban remains an open question. Both consolidated power through successive electoral victories while steadily subordinating independent institutions to executive preference.
India’s federal structure, regional diversity, and coalition rule complicate this level of consolidation for Modi. Powerful state governments in the south, a reenergized opposition, and an awakened youth population present structural obstacles that neither Erdogan nor Orban faced. The recent widespread detentions in New Delhi therefore do not signal absolute power; they appear as cracks in Modi’s strongman image, revealing a politician struggling to maintain control over a resilient democratic resistance.
The events unfolding on the streets of New Delhi mark the end of Modi’s unchallenged political dominance and the beginning of a volatile, high-stakes era. Eroding institutional independence makes his prolonged personal dominance both more feasible and more costly, as relying on brute force risks further eroding India’s reputation and angering citizens.
This moment will test whether India’s political system can absorb sustained discontent without further institutional damage. The voter list controversy has crystallized deeper questions about fairness and accountability. The scale of the police response has broadcast those questions more widely than any opposition program could have managed. How Modi chooses to answer—through dialogue or continued force—will shape the remainder of his third term and the future of India’s democracy.

sources.headline: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
sources.text: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest siteImage source, ReutersImage caption, The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement BySharanya HrishikeshBBC News, DelhiWhat is the point of a protest?To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen?For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi.But that may now be coming to an end.This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site.The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned.Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown.Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day.Delhi Police says, external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford.Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed.This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to itYellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand.In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions.Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined.Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament.Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament."Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper, external.Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years.Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes.Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause.It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance."It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra.Image source, Courtesy Rachna DhingraImage caption, In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheetsDipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme, the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar."It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says.Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise".But sustaining a protest for months was not easy.Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up.In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests.A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution.When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time."That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying.Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters.It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest.Those rules have become much stricter, external now.In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night."Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, In 2006, Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save the Narmada river movement) leader Medha Patkar (grey sari), sat on a 20-day hunger strike at Jantar MantarImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, In 2015, retired soldiers held protests at Jantar Mantar against the delay in the implementation of a pension schemeWhile Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture.Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance."We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says.When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said.She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar.She sees signs of that in protests by farmers who camped at Delhi's borders for months, and people who sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhood demanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law.Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi.It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site.Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed".As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?

sources.headline: Myanmar Establishes New Committee to Advance Normalization With ASEAN
sources.text:
Myanmar’s military-backed government has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee in order to support its efforts to reintegrate itself into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The Southeast Asian bloc has excluded Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings since late 2021, due to its failure to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus plan. Promulgated in April 2021, two months after a military coup, the Consensus calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid.
The Irrawaddy reported yesterday that the new body, which met for the first time on Tuesday, ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit next month, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the 11-nation organization. Tuesday’s meeting was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe and attended by representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare.
Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” from ASEAN since 2021, The Irrawaddy reported. The meeting also discussed “Myanmar‑led approaches” for restoring the country’s position in the bloc.
Since taking office in April, Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government has launched a diplomatic charm offensive, involving visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of much-needed foreign investment.
A priority has been the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Many of the latter’s member states appear to be supportive of Naypyidaw’s goal, and five of them – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.
The Philippines also appears to be softening. In a recent interview, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN for 2026, said that while the Five-Point Consensus was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a “new approach” on Myanmar.
At the same time as it has wooed individual ASEAN member states, the military-backed government has forcefully rejected the Five-Point Consensus. In July, Myanmar’s military proxy parliament adopted a motion rejecting the Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, which “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.” Min Aung Hlaing said in a speech the following month that some member states had “adopted positions and practices that it regarded as discriminatory towards Myanmar.”
While most member states are now leaning in the direction of reopening ASEAN’s door to Myanmar – Thailand and Malaysia have both explicitly stated that this is their goal, and Singapore and Timor-Leste appear to be the last hold-outs – full normalization, like all ASEAN decisions, will require a consensus among all 11 member states. As I noted earlier this week, however, there are “evidently still differences within ASEAN over how fast engagement should proceed, and to what end.”
Unless ASEAN agrees to abandon the Five-Point Consensus altogether, normalization would seem to require at least some effort to implement it, however nominal. With the Myanmar military ramping up its attacks on resistance groups and civilian populations accused of harboring them, this seems unlikely in the current circumstances.
